docs.title: Research Methods in the Age of AI
Graduate research methods for an AI-mediated world
docs.text:
This course combines traditional research methodology with contemporary computational tools, including Python, Google Colab, pretrained language models, and generative AI.

The course focuses on how researchers move from research questions to evidence: reviewing literature, selecting appropriate research designs, collecting and organizing data, analyzing results, evaluating AI-assisted workflows, and communicating findings.

Tools can assist research, but they cannot replace methodological judgment.

View the syllabus Explore the weekly schedule

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• Design Research

Develop research questions and hypotheses, evaluate scholarly evidence, and select appropriate sampling, measurement, survey, experimental, and quasi-experimental designs.

  • Analyze Data

Prepare, analyze, and interpret quantitative data using introductory statistical methods and reproducible Python workflows in Google Colab.

  • Work with AI

Use large language models and pretrained language models as research tools while learning how to evaluate their outputs, limitations, and appropriate uses.

  • Maintain Human Oversight

Verify analytical and AI-generated outputs, examine errors and limitations, protect sensitive information, and make defensible research decisions.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text:
Begin by examining how research is changing as AI, computation, and large language models become part of contemporary research workflows.

You will learn foundational concepts behind large language models and Transformers, become familiar with Google Colab and basic Python, and explore how pretrained language models can support research tasks such as literature screening and classification.

The goal is computational literacy, not software engineering. No prior programming experience is required.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text:
Move from tools to research decisions.

You will learn how research questions connect to sampling, measurement, surveys, randomized experiments, A/B testing, and quasi-experimental designs. Emphasis is placed on selecting and justifying a research design that provides appropriate evidence for the question being asked.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
Learn how research data are organized, prepared, analyzed, and interpreted.

You will work with data cleaning and introductory analytical approaches including correlation, t-tests, linear regression, analysis of variance, chi-square, and computational text and sentiment classification.

Most topics follow a concept → guided application structure, with greater emphasis on analytical reasoning and interpretation than on extensive programming.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
Bring the research process together through responsible analysis and communication.

You will consider AI ethics, reproducibility, limitations, appropriate human oversight, and the communication of analytical findings to academic, industry, technology, nonprofit, and other stakeholder audiences.

The course concludes with a group research project in which you will apply an appropriate analytical approach to an instructor-provided dataset and communicate what the evidence means.

docs.title: Course Format
docs.text:
The course is taught primarily through in-person concept sessions and selected synchronous computational laboratories.

A small number of laboratory sessions use Zoom when the digital environment provides specific instructional advantages, including screen sharing, live debugging, Google Colab demonstrations, and collaborative examination of computational workflows.

Session Type Primary Focus Concept sessions Research logic, design, interpretation, discussion, and methodological decision-making Computational laboratories Python, Google Colab, AI tools, data analysis, screen sharing, and live debugging Workshops Research design, analytical planning, interpretation, and stakeholder communication

docs.title: Course Tools
docs.text:
You will work with several contemporary research tools throughout the course:

  • Google Colab for browser-based Python notebooks
  • Python for introductory data management, analysis, and computational research
  • Pretrained language models for guided language-processing activities
  • Generative AI for selected research and coding activities
  • GitHub for openly accessible instructional materials and reproducible course resources

You are not expected to memorize Python syntax or become an AI engineer. The emphasis is on understanding what the tools are doing, when they are appropriate, and how their outputs should be evaluated.

docs.title: Begin Here
docs.text:
1. Review the course syllabus.
  2. Examine the weekly schedule.
  3. Read the AI use policy.
  4. Open the lecture materials.

docs.title: Guiding Principle
docs.text: AI may assist your research and coding, but it may not replace your understanding, judgment, validation, or responsibility.

docs.title: Permitted Uses
docs.text:
You may use approved AI systems to:

  • request explanations of code;
  • generate an initial code structure;
  • create test cases;
  • compare analytical approaches;
  • improve code readability;
  • review code for potential mistakes; and
  • explore alternative visualizations.

docs.title: Your Responsibilities
docs.text:
You must be able to:

  1. explain what your code is intended to do;
  2. identify the data and variables used;
  3. interpret the output;
  4. explain how the output was verified;
  5. identify possible errors and limitations; and
  6. modify the analysis when the data or research question changes.

docs.title: Required AI Documentation
docs.text:
For major assignments, you may be asked to document:

  • which AI tools you used;
  • what you asked the tools to do;
  • representative prompts or instructions;
  • what you changed; and
  • how you checked the outputs.

docs.title: Data Privacy
docs.text:
Do not upload any of the following to an external AI system:

  • personally identifiable information;
  • private or confidential information;
  • protected research-participant data;
  • proprietary datasets;
  • authentication credentials; or
  • API keys.

Never publish API keys

API keys must never appear in a notebook, public repository, screenshot,
lecture slide, or assignment submission.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Research methods are changing as computation, large language models, and increasingly accessible analytical tools become part of everyday research.

In this course, you will learn how to move from a research question to evidence: reviewing literature, selecting appropriate research designs, organizing and analyzing data, interpreting findings, evaluating AI-assisted workflows, and communicating results.

The course combines traditional research methodology with modern research tools, including Python, Google Colab, pretrained language models, and generative AI. Programming is treated as a research tool rather than as an end in itself. No prior programming experience is required.

Tools can assist research, but they cannot replace methodological judgment.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of the course, you should be able to:

  1. Explain the major stages of the research process and connect research questions to evidence, design, analysis, and interpretation.
  2. Explain foundational concepts behind contemporary AI and large language models at a level relevant to applied research.
  3. Use Google Colab and basic Python to conduct reproducible research tasks.
  4. Critically evaluate the use of AI and pretrained language models in research workflows.
  5. Develop research questions and hypotheses grounded in scholarly literature.
  6. Distinguish among major quantitative research designs, including surveys, experiments, A/B tests, and quasi-experiments.
  7. Identify appropriate sampling, measurement, and data-collection strategies.
  8. Select and conduct introductory statistical analyses including correlation, t-tests, regression, ANOVA, and chi-square.
  9. Apply introductory computational approaches to text data, including sentiment and text classification.
  10. Interpret analytical results in substantive rather than purely statistical terms.
  11. Identify ethical, validity, and reproducibility concerns associated with computational and AI-assisted research.
  12. Communicate research findings to academic, industry, and other stakeholder audiences.

docs.title: Block 1 — Modern Research Tools in the Age of AI
docs.text: You will begin by examining how AI and computation are changing contemporary research. Topics include large language models, Transformer foundations, Google Colab, Python fundamentals, pretrained language models, and human evaluation of AI-assisted research workflows.

docs.title: Block 2 — Data Collection and Research Design
docs.text: You will move from tools to research decisions, including research questions and hypotheses, sampling, measurement, surveys, randomized experiments, A/B testing, quasi-experimental designs, and validity.

docs.title: Block 3 — Data Analysis and Interpretation
docs.text:
You will learn how data are structured, prepared, analyzed, and interpreted. Topics include data cleaning, correlation, t-tests, linear regression, ANOVA, chi-square, and introductory computational text and sentiment classification.

Most analytical topics follow a concept → guided application structure, emphasizing methodological reasoning and interpretation over extensive programming.

docs.title: Block 4 — Responsible Research and Communication
docs.text:
You will integrate analytical reasoning with AI ethics, reproducibility, human oversight, limitations, and stakeholder communication.

The course concludes with an applied group research project in which you use an instructor-provided dataset, select an appropriate analytical approach, interpret the results, and communicate what the evidence means.

docs.title: Technology
docs.text:
You will work with:

  • Google Colab for browser-based computational notebooks
  • Python for introductory data management and analysis
  • pandas and NumPy for working with structured data
  • statistical Python libraries for introductory quantitative analysis
  • pretrained language models for guided computational text activities
  • generative AI for selected research and coding activities
  • GitHub for openly accessible instructional and computational materials

No prior programming experience is required.

You are not expected to memorize Python syntax or become an AI engineer. The emphasis is on understanding what computational tools are doing, when they are appropriate, and how their outputs should be evaluated.

docs.title: Course Readings
docs.text:
There is no required textbook to purchase.

Research methodology, computational tools, and AI are evolving quickly, and no single textbook adequately covers the full scope of the course. Readings are therefore selected from freely available books, scholarly articles, technical documentation, and instructor-provided materials.

One frequently used resource is:

Ethan Weed, Learning Statistics with Python

Specific readings are assigned according to the topics covered each week. You are not expected to read an entire technical book from beginning to end.

View course readings and resources

docs.title: Assessments
docs.text:
Assessments are aligned with the four course blocks.

Assessment Learning Focus Weight Colab Access Check Preparation for Block 1 5% Human + AI Literature Screening Exercise Block 1: Modern Research Tools 15% Block 1 Knowledge Assessment Block 1: Modern Research Tools 20% Research Design Brief Block 2: Data Collection and Research Design 20% Final Project Analysis Plan Blocks 3–4: Analysis and Responsible Research 10% Final Stakeholder Research Presentation Blocks 3–4: Analysis, Interpretation, and Communication 30% Total 100%

The assessment sequence moves from understanding and evaluating modern research tools, to making research-design decisions, to conducting and communicating an applied analysis.

docs.title: AI and Human Oversight
docs.text:
AI is intentionally incorporated into selected course activities.

You will learn to use AI systems as research tools whose outputs require evaluation, rather than as substitutes for research judgment.

Depending on the activity, AI may support:

  • literature organization;
  • classification;
  • coding;
  • debugging;
  • computational analysis; or
  • other research workflows.

You remain responsible for:

  • verifying AI-generated information and code;
  • understanding the analyses you conduct;
  • identifying errors and limitations;
  • protecting sensitive information;
  • documenting AI use when appropriate; and
  • making the final methodological and interpretive decisions.

docs.text:
These public pages provide an overview of the major learning activities and preparation materials for the course.

Assignment What You Do What It Demonstrates Colab Access Check Set up access to Google Colab and confirm that you can open and use a computational notebook. Readiness to work in a cloud-based research environment Human + AI Literature Screening Exercise Work with a research question, identify peer-reviewed studies, make your own relevance judgments, and compare those judgments with classifications produced by a pretrained language model. Human oversight, literature evaluation, AI-assisted research, and model validation Block 1 Knowledge Assessment Demonstrate understanding of modern research tools, foundational LLM concepts, computational environments, basic Python interpretation, and limitations of AI-assisted workflows. Conceptual understanding of contemporary computational and AI-enabled research Research Design Brief Develop a concise research proposal that connects a research question or hypothesis to scholarly literature, sampling, measurement, and an appropriate research design. Research design reasoning, methodological justification, and critical consideration of AI use Final Project Analysis Plan Work with an instructor-provided dataset and research question to identify relevant variables, select an analytical method, and justify the proposed workflow. Analytical planning and the ability to connect research questions, data, and methods Final Stakeholder Research Presentation Conduct an analysis in Python/Google Colab, interpret the results, identify limitations, reflect on any AI-assisted coding or debugging, and communicate the findings to a stakeholder audience. Data analysis, interpretation, responsible AI use, reproducibility, and research communication

docs.title: Assignment Philosophy
docs.text:
The assignments are designed to move progressively from:

tool literacy → research design → analysis → interpretation and communication

Across the course, the emphasis is not simply on whether a computational or AI tool produces an answer. You should also be able to explain:

  • why a research approach is appropriate;
  • what the computational or AI tool is doing;
  • how you verified the output;
  • what limitations remain; and
  • what the evidence means for the research question.

Official submission instructions, deadlines, and grading information are provided separately to enrolled students.

docs.title: How to Use the Codebooks
docs.text:
During class, the codebooks may be used for live demonstrations and guided computational activities.

You are encouraged to:

  • open the relevant codebook before or during class;
  • follow along as each step is demonstrated;
  • run the code in your own Colab environment;
  • add comments or notes explaining what each step does;
  • experiment with small changes to understand how the workflow behaves; and
  • return to the codebooks later as references for assignments and projects.

The emphasis is on understanding what the code is doing, why it is being used, and how to evaluate the output.

docs.title: Exploring TikTok User Experience with Python
docs.text:
In today's lab, you will practice using Python to organize, retrieve, transform, and process information from a fictional TikTok user-experience study.

The goal is not to conduct an actual TikTok analysis. Instead, you will practice translating a research-related problem into a small computational workflow.

You will work in Google Colab and may use an AI assistant to help you understand code, debug errors, or develop a solution.

Today's Goal

You are not expected to memorize Python syntax. Focus on understanding what the code is doing, why it works, and how you can verify the result.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Open a new Google Colab notebook:

Open Google Colab

Rename your notebook:

JOUR701_Week3Lab_YourName

At the top of your notebook, create a Markdown cell containing:

Name:
Assigned Activity:

docs.title: How Today's Lab Works
docs.text:
Each group will be assigned two primary activities.

Your job is to:

  1. Read the task carefully.
  2. Think about what Python needs to do.
  3. Write or modify the code.
  4. Run the code.
  5. Inspect the output.
  6. Use AI assistance if needed.
  7. Verify that your solution actually answers the task.
  8. Be prepared to share your screen and explain your process.

If you finish early, try the Challenge activity.

docs.title: Using AI During the Lab
docs.text:
You may use ChatGPT or another approved AI assistant.

AI can help you:

  • explain unfamiliar code
  • give you a hint
  • interpret an error message
  • suggest a correction
  • review your solution
  • simplify complicated code
  • suggest ways to test your result

However:

AI-generated code is a proposed solution, not a verified solution.

When you use AI, add a Markdown cell to your notebook:

AI prompt I used:

What AI suggested:

What I changed or used:

How I verified the result:

You may ask AI for the full code if that is useful, but you should still be able to explain what the important parts of the code are doing.

docs.title: Activity 1: Explore User Comments
docs.text:
A researcher collected several comments about users' TikTok experiences.

Copy this into your notebook:

comments = [
    "I keep finding videos that match my interests",
    "There are too many ads now",
    "The For You page feels repetitive",
    "I like discovering new creators",
    "Sometimes I lose track of time while scrolling"
]

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
Without running the code first, predict what each operation should return.

Then use Python to:

  1. Retrieve the first comment.
  2. Retrieve the last comment.
  3. Retrieve the second and third comments.
  4. Retrieve the first three comments.
  5. Find the total number of comments.

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
• Why does Python start counting at 0?
  • Why does a slice such as [1:3] not include index 3?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Show one prediction you made before running the code and explain whether your prediction was correct.

docs.title: Activity 2: Clean a User Comment
docs.text:
A comment was entered with inconsistent capitalization and extra spaces.

comment = "   I LOVE Discovering New Creators!   "

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
Transform the comment so that it becomes:

i love discovering new creators!

Then replace:

creators

with:

accounts

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
• Which string methods did you use?
  • What object was each method acting on?
  • Does the order of your operations matter?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Explain your sequence of operations and why you chose that order.

docs.title: Activity 3: Build a User Record
docs.text:
Imagine one participant in a TikTok user-experience study provided the following information:

Participant: P07
Daily use: 95 minutes
Primary reason: entertainment
Uses For You page: yes
Reported distraction: yes

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
1. Represent this participant as a Python dictionary.
  2. Retrieve the participant's daily use.
  3. Retrieve the participant's primary reason for using TikTok.
  4. Add the following information to the dictionary:
Age group: 18–24

docs.title: Think About
docs.text: Why might this structure be more useful than storing all the participant information in one sentence?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Explain the difference between a key and a value in your dictionary.

docs.title: Activity 4: Navigate Multiple User Records
docs.text:
A researcher has information from several participants:

users = [
    {
        "participant": "P01",
        "daily_minutes": 45,
        "primary_reason": "entertainment"
    },
    {
        "participant": "P02",
        "daily_minutes": 120,
        "primary_reason": "news"
    },
    {
        "participant": "P03",
        "daily_minutes": 75,
        "primary_reason": "entertainment"
    }
]

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
Use Python to:

  1. Retrieve the complete record for the first participant.
  2. Retrieve P02's primary reason for using TikTok.
  3. Retrieve P03's daily minutes.
  4. Retrieve the final participant record without using its numerical position from the beginning.

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
What kind of Python structure is users?

How are a list and dictionary being combined?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Explain how Python moves through the nested structure to retrieve one specific value.

docs.title: Activity 5: Process Every Participant
docs.text:
Use the following records:

users = [
    {"participant": "P01", "daily_minutes": 45},
    {"participant": "P02", "daily_minutes": 120},
    {"participant": "P03", "daily_minutes": 75},
    {"participant": "P04", "daily_minutes": 150}
]

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
1. Print every participant ID.
  2. Print every participant ID together with their reported daily minutes.
  3. Modify your code so that only participants reporting more than 90 minutes are printed.

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
In this code:

for user in users:

what does user represent during each repetition?

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
The 90-minute threshold is being used only to practice Python conditions.

It is not a scientifically justified threshold for defining problematic or excessive TikTok use.

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Explain what part of your code repeats and what part makes a decision.

docs.title: Activity 6: Find Comments About the Algorithm
docs.text:
Consider these comments:

comments = [
    "The algorithm knows what I like",
    "I mostly follow my friends",
    "The For You page feels repetitive",
    "I don't understand how the algorithm chooses videos",
    "The ads interrupt my experience"
]

Python can test whether one piece of text appears inside another:

"algorithm" in comment.lower()

This produces either:

True

or:

False

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
1. Print only comments containing the word "algorithm".
  2. Count how many comments contain "algorithm".

You may find this useful:

count = 0

and:

count += 1

count += 1 means:

count = count + 1

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
Why might we use:

comment.lower()

before searching for the word?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Explain how your loop, condition, and string method work together.

docs.title: Activity 7: Create a Reusable Cleaning Function
docs.text:
Consider:

comment = "   The FOR YOU Page Feels Repetitive   "

docs.title: Your Task
docs.text:
Create a function called:

clean_comment()

that:

  • removes spaces from the beginning and end
  • converts the text to lowercase
  • returns the cleaned comment

Then use the same function on the following comments:

comments = [
    "   I LOVE Finding New Creators ",
    "The ALGORITHM Knows Me Too Well   ",
    "   Too Many ADS!   "
]

docs.title: Think About
docs.text: Why might creating one reusable function be preferable to repeatedly writing the same cleaning commands?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Show your function and explain what goes in and what comes out.

docs.title: Activity 8: Debug a Research Workflow
docs.text:
The following code is supposed to print participants who report more than 90 minutes of TikTok use.

However, it contains several problems.

users = [
    {"participant": "P01", "minutes": 45},
    {"participant": "P02", "minutes": 110},
    {"participant": "P03", "minutes": 75}
]

for user in users
    if user["Minutes"] > 90:
    print(user["participant"])

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
1. Run the code.
  2. Read the error message.
  3. Fix the first problem.
  4. Run the code again.
  5. Continue until the code works correctly.
  6. Identify each problem you found.

docs.title: Using AI
docs.text:
Try asking:

Explain this Python error one problem at a time.
Do not rewrite the entire solution.

docs.title: Think About
docs.text: Why might fixing one error reveal another error?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Show us one error you encountered and explain how you identified the problem.

docs.title: Activity 9: Evaluate AI-Generated Code
docs.text:
Imagine you asked an AI assistant:

Find all participants who use TikTok for more than 90 minutes.

The AI generated:

heavy_users = [
    user["participant"]
    for user in users
    if user["minutes"] > 90
]

docs.title: Your Tasks
docs.text:
Without asking AI immediately:

  1. Run the code.
  2. Inspect the result.
  3. Decide whether it appears to solve the task.
  4. Identify which parts of the code you understand.
  5. Identify anything you cannot explain.

Then ask AI:

Rewrite this using a regular for loop and if statement.
Explain how the two versions accomplish the same task.

docs.title: Think About
docs.text:
• Is shorter code always better?
  • Would you use code in a research project if you could not explain how it works?

docs.title: If You Share Your Screen
docs.text: Compare the original AI-generated solution with the simpler version.

docs.text:
1. Display the final participant record.
  2. Retrieve only P02's comment.
  3. Print every participant ID.
  4. Print participants with more than 90 minutes of use.

docs.title: Screen Sharing
docs.text:
During class, teams will be invited to share their screens.

When you share, briefly show:

  1. Your task
  2. What you tried
  3. Your code
  4. Any error or challenge you encountered
  5. How you used AI, if applicable
  6. Your final output
  7. How you verified the result

You do not need to have a perfect solution to share.

Debugging, unexpected results, and alternative solutions are useful parts of the learning process.

docs.title: After Class
docs.text:
A worked solution notebook will be posted after the lab.

View Week 3 Lab Solutions in Google Colab

  • compare approaches
  • review code you found difficult
  • understand errors
  • try activities you were not assigned
  • revisit the lab before future computational exercises

Note

The solution notebook provides one possible approach. Python problems often have multiple valid solutions. Focus on whether the code correctly performs the intended operation and whether you can understand and explain the workflow.

docs.title: What You Practiced
docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you should have practiced how to:

  • organize information using lists and dictionaries
  • retrieve information using indexes and keys
  • transform text using string methods
  • process multiple records using loops
  • apply simple rules using conditions
  • combine Python structures into small workflows
  • create a reusable function
  • interpret and debug errors
  • use AI as a coding assistant
  • verify AI-generated code

docs.title: Week 4 Lab: AI-Assisted Literature Prioritization with Hugging Face + Colab
Overview
docs.text:
In this lab, you will explore how a pretrained Transformer model can help prioritize candidate literature for a research question.

The goal is not to automate or replace a systematic literature review. Instead, you will examine where AI-assisted screening may be useful, where human judgment remains necessary, and what kinds of evidence would be needed before relying on a model for literature screening.

By the end of the lab, you should be able to:

  • Load a literature dataset into Google Colab
  • Use a pretrained Hugging Face model to classify article abstracts
  • Compare your own judgment with the model's judgment
  • Examine disagreements between human and model decisions
  • Revise classification labels and evaluate whether the output improves
  • Save model results for review and submission

docs.title: 1. Prepare Your Group Dataset
docs.text:
Each group should have:

  • One research question
  • 3 peer-reviewed article abstracts per person
  • About 12–15 abstracts total for a group of 4–5
  • One combined .csv file
  • Abstracts from peer-reviewed journal articles only

Your CSV file should include at least these columns:

Group Member,abstract
Max,"This study examines how journalists use generative AI in daily work..."
Alex,"Using survey data, this study explores how young adults encounter news..."
Sarah,"This article analyzes how platform users evaluate health misinformation..."

Each student's name should appear next to the abstracts they personally contributed.

docs.title: 2. Open Google Colab and Upload Your CSV
docs.text:
Open a new Google Colab notebook.

Upload your group's CSV file to Colab.

Then load the file using pandas:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("your_file_name.csv")

df.head()

Check that:

  • The file loads correctly
  • Each row contains one abstract
  • The correct group member is listed for each abstract

docs.title: 3. Human Judgment Comes First
docs.text:
Before looking at any AI output, return to the 3 abstracts you personally contributed.

Read each abstract yourself and decide how relevant it is to your group's research question.

Use one of these labels:

  • Clearly relevant
  • Possibly relevant
  • Probably unrelated

Record your judgment before running the model.

Do not change your original judgment after seeing what the AI predicts.

The purpose is to compare your own reasoning with the model's reasoning later.

docs.title: 4. Define the Classification Task
docs.text:
The model does not independently know what your research question means by "relevant."

You must define the possible labels.

For example, imagine your research question is:

How is generative AI changing journalists' professional practices?

You might begin with labels such as:

candidate_labels = [
    "relevant to the research question",
    "not relevant to the research question"
]

These labels tell the model what kinds of categories it should compare against.

docs.title: 5. Load a Pretrained Hugging Face Model
docs.text:
We will use a pretrained model through Hugging Face's pipeline() function.

from transformers import pipeline

Create a zero-shot classification pipeline:

classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli"
)

This allows us to give the model an abstract and a set of possible labels without training a new model ourselves.

docs.title: 6. Try One Abstract First
docs.text:
Before processing the full dataset, test the model on one abstract.

abstract = df.loc[0, "abstract"]

result = classifier(
    abstract,
    candidate_labels
)

result

Look at:

  • Which label received the highest score?
  • How confident was the model?
  • Does the prediction make sense based on your research question?

Ask yourself:

Do you agree or disagree with the model? Why?

docs.title: 7. Process the Full Abstract Dataset
docs.text:
Once your group understands how the model works, apply it to the full dataset.

One simple approach is:

def classify_abstract(text):
    result = classifier(
        text,
        candidate_labels
    )

    return result["labels"][0]

Then apply the function to each abstract:

df["AI Judgment"] = df["abstract"].apply(classify_abstract)

Preview the results:

df.head()

docs.title: 8. Compare Your Judgment with the AI Judgment
docs.text:
Now return to the 3 abstracts you personally contributed.

For each of your abstracts:

  1. Compare your original human judgment with the AI judgment.
  2. Decide whether you agree with the AI.
  3. Record Yes or No.
  4. Write a short explanation.

If you agree with the AI:

  • Explain what evidence in the abstract supports the AI judgment.

If you disagree with the AI:

  • Explain what the model may have misunderstood, overlooked, or interpreted incorrectly.

If you are unsure:

  • Discuss that abstract with your group.
  • Listen to your peers' reasoning.
  • Then make your own final Yes/No decision.

You are responsible for completing the rows corresponding to your own abstracts.

Your table should look like this:

Group Member Abstract Human Judgment AI Judgment Agree with AI? Reason Alex ... Clearly relevant Relevant Yes The abstract directly examines AI use in journalistic work. Maya ... Possibly relevant Not relevant No The model may have missed the connection between automation and newsroom practice.

docs.title: 9. Change the Labels
docs.text:
The first labels you choose may be too broad.

Now revise the candidate labels so they better reflect your research question.

For example, instead of:

candidate_labels = [
    "relevant",
    "not relevant"
]

you might try:

candidate_labels = [
    "directly examines generative AI in journalists' professional work",
    "mentions journalism but does not examine generative AI use",
    "not related to the research question"
]

Run the model again using your updated labels.

Ask:

  • Did the predictions become more useful?
  • Did any previous disagreements disappear?
  • Did new disagreements appear?
  • Why might changing the labels change the model's judgment?

docs.title: 10. Run the Updated Model on the Full Dataset
docs.text:
Apply the revised labels to the full abstract dataset.

For example:

def classify_abstract_updated(text):
    result = classifier(
        text,
        candidate_labels
    )

    return result["labels"][0]

Then:

df["Updated AI Judgment"] = df["abstract"].apply(
    classify_abstract_updated
)

Preview the results:

df.head()

docs.title: 11. Save Your Results
docs.text:
Save your completed dataset as a new CSV file.

df.to_csv(
    "week4_ai_literature_results.csv",
    index=False
)

Download the file from Colab and make sure your group keeps a copy.

docs.title: 12. Final Human–AI Comparison
docs.text:
After running the updated model, review your own abstracts again.

For each abstract you contributed, your final table should include:

  • Group member name
  • Abstract
  • Your original human judgment
  • AI judgment
  • Agree with AI: Yes or No
  • Brief reason

Your reason should explain why you agree or disagree.

Do not simply write:

Yes, I agree.

Instead, connect your explanation to the abstract and the research question.

For example:

Yes. The abstract directly examines how journalists use generative AI in their daily professional workflow.

Or:

No. The abstract discusses digital journalism broadly, but it does not examine generative AI use, which is central to our research question.

docs.title: 13. Discuss One Interesting Disagreement
docs.text:
As a group, identify one disagreement that you think is especially useful or interesting.

Be prepared to briefly explain:

  • Your research question
  • The abstract
  • The human judgment
  • The model judgment
  • Whether the human reviewer agreed or disagreed with the AI
  • Why the disagreement may have occurred
  • What you would do next as a researcher

Possible reasons for disagreement include:

  • The abstract is genuinely ambiguous
  • The labels are too broad
  • The labels are poorly defined
  • Important context is missing from the abstract
  • The model focused on the wrong words
  • Human reviewers interpreted the research question differently

docs.title: Assignment 2 Deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one agreement table file per group on Blackboard.

Due: 5:00 PM tomorrow

The file should include:

Group Member Abstract Human Judgment AI Judgment Agree with AI? Reason

Although the group submits one combined file, each student is responsible for the rows corresponding to the abstracts they personally contributed.

Your individual portion will be evaluated based on whether you:

  • Completed your assigned abstracts
  • Made a clear human judgment
  • Compared that judgment with the model
  • Provided a meaningful Yes/No agreement decision
  • Explained your reasoning using evidence from the abstract and the research question

docs.title: Before You Leave
docs.text:
Consider this question:

Would you allow this model to automatically exclude papers from your literature review?

Think about:

  • Why or why not?
  • What kinds of errors would matter most?
  • What evidence would you need before trusting the model?
  • Where should human judgment remain in the workflow?

docs.title: Key Takeaway
docs.text:
AI can help researchers screen and prioritize abstracts, especially when working with larger collections of literature.

However, human judgment is still needed to:

  • Define what relevance means
  • Evaluate ambiguous cases
  • Interpret disagreements
  • Refine classification labels
  • Protect against accidentally excluding important studies

A reproducible Python workflow makes AI-assisted literature screening easier to inspect, critique, compare, and improve.

docs.title: Online Books and Course Readings
docs.text:
This course does not rely on a single textbook. Instead, readings are drawn from openly available books, scholarly articles, technical documentation, and other research resources.

Specific required readings will be identified on the relevant weekly course pages. The resources below also serve as optional references if you want additional explanation, examples, or technical practice.

docs.title: Learning Statistics with Python
docs.text:
Danielle Navarro and Ethan Weed

Open Learning Statistics with Python

This is the primary introductory resource used across the course. It connects research design, Python, data management, visualization, statistical reasoning, and commonly used quantitative analyses.

Selected sections may support topics including:

  • Python fundamentals
  • research design
  • descriptive statistics
  • data visualization
  • data wrangling
  • hypothesis testing
  • comparison of means
  • categorical analysis
  • ANOVA
  • linear regression

docs.title: Python for Data Analysis, Third Edition
docs.text:
Wes McKinney

Open Python for Data Analysis

This resource provides more detailed instruction on Python, computational notebooks, NumPy, pandas, data loading, data cleaning, data restructuring, aggregation, and analysis.

Selected sections may supplement laboratory activities involving data preparation, DataFrames, data cleaning, and reproducible analytical workflows.

docs.title: Python Data Science Handbook
docs.text:
Jake VanderPlas

Open the Python Data Science Handbook

This book provides additional examples involving Python, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, and data-science workflows.

It is primarily an optional technical reference for anyone who wants more explanation, additional examples, or further practice beyond what is required in class.

docs.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python
docs.text:
Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani, and Jonathan Taylor

Open An Introduction to Statistical Learning

This resource provides a broader introduction to statistical modeling and contemporary analytical approaches.

Selected sections may be used as supplementary references for topics such as regression, classification, model interpretation, and the distinction between explanation and prediction. More advanced material in the book extends beyond the scope of this course.

How readings will be assigned

You are not expected to read these books in full.

Required chapters, sections, articles, or documentation will be identified on the relevant weekly course page. Materials not specifically assigned should be treated as optional reference resources.

docs.title: Python and Data Analysis
docs.text:
Official documentation can be especially useful when you need to understand how a particular function, library, or analytical method works.

  • Python Documentation
  • pandas Documentation
  • NumPy Documentation
  • SciPy Documentation
  • statsmodels Documentation
  • Matplotlib Documentation

docs.title: Google Colab
docs.text:
Open Google Colab

Google Colab is the primary computational environment used in the course. It allows you to write and run Python in a browser without installing a local programming environment.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
Open GitHub

GitHub is used throughout this public course site to organize instructional materials, examples, and reproducible computational resources.

docs.title: Hugging Face
docs.text:
Open Hugging Face

Hugging Face provides access to pretrained language models, datasets, documentation, and open-source tools.

You will encounter pretrained models in selected course activities involving model access, classification, text analysis, and evaluation of AI-assisted research workflows.

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
Selected generative AI tools may be used for activities such as:

  • coding assistance
  • debugging
  • research organization
  • classification support
  • methodological critique
  • interpretation of computational workflows

The specific tools used may vary as AI systems and access conditions evolve.

The emphasis throughout the course is not simply on obtaining an AI-generated answer, but on evaluating the output, identifying limitations, and maintaining human oversight.

docs.title: Research and Scholarly Resources
docs.text:
Depending on the research question and activity, you may also use:

  • university library databases
  • peer-reviewed scholarly journals
  • research-methods references
  • statistical consulting resources
  • writing support resources
  • accessibility resources
  • official technical documentation

When conducting literature-based work, prioritize original peer-reviewed research and evaluate the relevance and credibility of sources rather than relying solely on AI-generated summaries.

docs.title: Getting Technical Help
docs.text:
Debugging is a normal part of computational research.

When requesting technical help—from the instructor, a classmate, documentation, or an AI coding assistant—try to provide:

  1. Your objective — What are you trying to accomplish?
  2. The relevant data — What variables or data structure are involved?
  3. Your code — What did you run?
  4. The error — What happened?
  5. Your expectation — What did you expect to happen?
  6. What you already tried — What changes or solutions have you tested?

Providing this information makes it much easier to diagnose the problem and, more importantly, helps you develop a reproducible approach to computational problem-solving.
